summary.text: A digit identity modulo divisors of 81 shows that, for \(d=9t\mid81\), divisibility of a positive number and its reversal by \(d\) forces its digit sum to be divisible by \(d\); the digit-sum bound then gives \(N\ge10^t-1\), with the all-nines candidates proving the exact cases \(d=9,27,81\). For larger exponents, start with the 11-digit palindrome \(29799999792\), divisible by \(3^5\), and repeatedly concatenate three copies: the multiplier \(1+10^m+10^{2m}\) supplies another factor of 3 while preserving palindromicity, and the resulting length \(11\cdot3^k<3^{k+3}\) makes this witness smaller than the corresponding all-nines number.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(N)\) denote the nonnegative integer obtained by reversing the ordinary base-10 digits of \(N\). For a positive integer \(d\), call \(N\) admissible for \(d\) if
\[
N>0,\qquad d\mid N,\qquad d\mid \operatorname{rev}(N).
\]
Then \(a(d)\) is the least admissible integer for \(d\), whenever one exists. In particular, if \(N\) is admissible, then \(a(d)\le N\); and if, in addition, every admissible \(M\) satisfies \(N\le M\), then \(a(d)=N\).

We first prove a digit-sum lemma that will provide the exact lower bounds needed for \(d=9,27,81\).

Write a finite list of decimal digits in least-significant-first order as
\[
L=(b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_{\ell-1}),
\]
and put
\[
[L]_{10}=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}b_i10^i,
\qquad
S(L)=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}b_i.
\]
The number represented by the reversed list is
\[
[L^{\mathrm{rev}}]_{10}=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}b_i10^{\ell-1-i}.
\]
Modulo \(81\), for every \(j\ge0\),
\[
10^j=(1+9)^j\equiv 1+9j\pmod {81},
\]
because every binomial term involving \(9^2\) is divisible by \(81\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
10\bigl([L]_{10}+[L^{\mathrm{rev}}]_{10}\bigr)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}b_i\bigl(10^{i+1}+10^{\ell-i}\bigr)\\
&\equiv \sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}b_i\bigl((1+9(i+1))+(1+9(\ell-i))\bigr)\\
&=(11+9\ell)S(L)\pmod {81}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
The same congruence is valid modulo every divisor \(d\) of \(81\).

Suppose now that \(d\mid81\), and that both \([L]_{10}\) and \([L^{\mathrm{rev}}]_{10}\) are divisible by \(d\). Equation (1), reduced modulo \(d\), gives
\[
(11+9\ell)S(L)\equiv0\pmod d.
\]
Every prime divisor of \(d\) is \(3\), whereas
\[
11+9\ell\equiv2\pmod3.
\]
Thus \(11+9\ell\) is relatively prime to \(d\), so it can be cancelled modulo \(d\). We conclude that
\[
d\mid S(L).
\tag{2}
\]
In words: if \(d\mid81\) divides a number and its decimal reversal, then \(d\) divides the sum of the decimal digits of that number.

We next derive a sharp lower bound from (2). Let
\[
d=9t,
\]
assume \(d\mid81\), and let \(N\) be admissible for \(d\). We claim that
\[
N\ge 10^t-1.
\tag{3}
\]
Suppose to the contrary that \(N<10^t-1\). In particular \(N<10^t\), so the ordinary decimal expansion of \(N\) has at most \(t\) digits. Let its digit list be \(L\), of length \(\ell\le t\). Since \(N>0\), its digit sum \(S(L)\) is positive. By (2), \(d=9t\) divides \(S(L)\), and hence
\[
S(L)\ge9t.
\]
On the other hand, every decimal digit is at most \(9\), so
\[
S(L)\le9\ell\le9t.
\]
All these inequalities must therefore be equalities. Hence \(\ell=t\), the digit sum is \(9t\), and every one of the \(t\) digits equals \(9\). It follows that
\[
N=\underbrace{99\cdots9}_{t\text{ digits}}=10^t-1,
\]
contrary to the supposition. This proves (3).

We can now determine the three exceptional values.

For \(d=9\), take \(t=1\). The number
\[
10^1-1=9
\]
is positive, is divisible by \(9\), and is unchanged by reversal. It is therefore admissible. Bound (3) says every admissible number is at least \(9\), so
\[
a(9)=9=10^{3^{2-2}}-1.
\]

For \(d=27\), take \(t=3\). The number
\[
10^3-1=999=27\cdot37
\]
is positive and unchanged by reversal, so it is admissible for \(27\). Again (3) proves minimality, giving
\[
a(27)=999=10^{3^{3-2}}-1.
\]

For \(d=81\), take \(t=9\). The number
\[
10^9-1=999{,}999{,}999=81\cdot12{,}345{,}679
\]
is positive and unchanged by reversal, so it is admissible for \(81\). Bound (3) again gives the matching lower bound, and therefore
\[
a(81)=999{,}999{,}999=10^{3^{4-2}}-1.
\]
Thus the asserted equality holds for \(n=2,3,4\).

It remains to show that it fails for every \(n\ge5\). For this we construct, for each \(k\ge0\), an explicit decimal palindrome \(V_k\) such that
\[
3^{k+5}\mid V_k
\tag{4}
\]
and such that \(V_k\) has only \(11\cdot3^k\) decimal digits.

Begin with the 11-digit palindrome
\[
V_0=29{,}799{,}999{,}792.
\]
Its digit word, read in either direction, is
\[
W_0=29799999792.
\]
Direct arithmetic gives
\[
29{,}799{,}999{,}792
 =243\cdot122{,}633{,}744
 =3^5\cdot122{,}633{,}744.
\]
Thus \(V_0\) is positive, palindromic, has 11 digits, and is divisible by \(3^5\).

Define the later digit words recursively by triple repetition:
\[
W_{k+1}=W_kW_kW_k,
\]
and let \(V_k\) be the integer represented by \(W_k\). Equivalently, \(W_k\) consists of \(3^k\) consecutive copies of \(W_0\). Therefore its length is
\[
m_k=11\cdot3^k.
\tag{5}
\]
The initial and final digits are both \(2\), so these words are genuine decimal expansions with no leading zero. Also, since \(W_0\) is a palindrome, every repeated word \(W_k\) is a palindrome. Thus
\[
\operatorname{rev}(V_k)=V_k.
\tag{6}
\]

We prove (4) by induction. It holds at \(k=0\) by the displayed factorization of \(V_0\). If \(W_k\) has length \(m_k\), concatenating three copies gives
\[
V_{k+1}=V_k\bigl(1+10^{m_k}+10^{2m_k}\bigr).
\tag{7}
\]
Since \(10\equiv1\pmod3\),
\[
1+10^{m_k}+10^{2m_k}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Thus the factor in parentheses in (7) is divisible by \(3\). If \(3^{k+5}\mid V_k\), equation (7) then implies
\[
3^{k+6}\mid V_{k+1}.
\]
This completes the induction.

It follows from (4) and (6) that \(V_k\) is admissible for \(3^{k+5}\): it is positive, both it and its reversal are divisible by \(3^{k+5}\), and in fact the two numbers are equal. Hence
\[
a(3^{k+5})\le V_k.
\tag{8}
\]

We compare this candidate with the proposed all-nines value. By (5), the number of digits of \(V_k\) is \(11\cdot3^k\), while
\[
3^{k+3}=27\cdot3^k.
\]
Because \(11<27\),
\[
11\cdot3^k<3^{k+3}.
\tag{9}
\]
Any positive integer having \(m_k\) decimal digits is less than \(10^{m_k}\). Using (9), we therefore obtain
\[
V_k<10^{m_k}\le 10^{3^{k+3}-1}<10^{3^{k+3}}-1.
\]
Combining this with (8) yields
\[
a(3^{k+5})<10^{3^{k+3}}-1.
\tag{10}
\]
In particular, equality with the all-nines number is impossible for every exponent of the form \(k+5\).

Finally, let \(n\ge2\). If \(n=2,3,4\), the three exact evaluations above show that
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Conversely, suppose this equality holds. If \(n\) were not one of \(2,3,4\), then, because \(n\ge2\), we would have \(n\ge5\). Put \(k=n-5\). Then
\[
k+5=n,\qquad k+3=n-2,
\]
and (10) becomes
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1,
\]
contradicting the assumed equality. Therefore \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\).

Hence, for every integer \(n\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{\ a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.\ }
\]
